source.title: Influence Dynamics and Stagewise Data Attribution
source.authors: J. Lee; Matthew Smith; Maxwell Adam; Jesse Hoogland

record.tranche_reason: Measures induction-head scores and induction-pattern influence over training, using a different experimental setup from the original sources; it does not reproduce their experiments.
record.gate_note: The study measures induction scores in a scratch-trained 14M Pythia model and in 3M-parameter intervention experiments. It does not measure loss by token index, a sharp in-context-learning gain, or a training-loss bump. The Pythia checkpoint BIF results and the toy-model influence results do not themselves measure induction-head behavior, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: In appendices D.3–D.4 the study tracks attention-head induction scores over training in a scratch-trained Pythia-14M run and in a 3M-parameter transformer. It also varies when induction-pattern tokens are upweighted and measures how that changes the timing of induction-head formation. This bears on V2, V4 and V5 with a method different from the originals. Its main contribution (Bayesian influence function dynamics) is not itself a measure of induction-head behaviour.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it omits the main conclusion. The authors conclude that training-data influence is stagewise and non-monotonic, with sign flips and peaks at developmental transitions such as induction-circuit formation. On induction specifically, BIF dynamics predict when upweighting induction patterns accelerates formation (a receptive window) versus delays or disrupts it (too early).
record.recipe_differences: Uses Bayesian influence estimates and induction-score measurements in Pythia-derived language models, with synthetic repeated sequences and timed data-weighting interventions; it is not a reproduction of the original induction-head experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect of induction-pattern upweighting varies by training window: early windows delay or disrupt learning, the 2k–2.5k window has little effect, and 4k–4.5k and 5k–5.5k windows accelerate it. The 14M scratch run uses a different data order and hardware from the original Pythia-14M run.

fits_no_version.finding: In public Pythia-14M checkpoints, the average BIF between induction-pattern tokens has an inflection around step 128, strengthens to about 30k steps, then falls.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data influence between induction-pattern tokens changes non-monotonically and tracks induction-circuit development.

fits_no_version.finding: In the scratch Pythia-14M run, BIF between repeated-segment tokens rises sharply then peaks; non-repeated pairs show no change (Fig. 16). Influence is not a rate of induction behaviour.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Influence-function peaks mark the induction-head transition.

record.problems: The induction-score plots provide no numerical values in the text. The induction timing in the 3M control is described as a peak at 9k in the results text but approximately 7k in the Figure 17 caption. Only Pythia-derived settings are tested. The intervention intentionally upweights induction-pattern data, so its effects do not by themselves establish uninduced behavior.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant induction-head behavior results were left out. The general Pythia token-class BIF plots and toy-model influence results were excluded because they do not measure induction-head behavior.

untested.parts: Composition with a previous-token head, and the mechanism in attention-only models. Only induction scores are measured, in models with MLPs.
The simultaneous sharp in-context-learning gain (loss by token index) and the bump in the training loss are not measured.
Only Pythia-style LMs at 14M and 3M. No other families, architectures or modalities.
Data-distribution properties (e.g. burstiness) and whether in-context learning persists are not varied or measured. Only the timing of loss upweighting is varied.

record.verdict_notes: Induction results are appendix-only and figure-heavy; no numeric induction scores appear in the text beyond the axis range (about 0 to 0.15). The 3M architecture (attention-only or not) is not stated. There are internal inconsistencies: the 9k peak in the text versus about 7k formation in the caption, and 'five' runs versus six listed windows. The upweighting deliberately emphasises induction data, but the outcome measured is natural head formation under an altered training setup, so it is treated as bearing on V5. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures induction scores but does not test whether the heads compose with an earlier previous-token head or directly analyze the attention pattern that implements [A][B] … [A] → [B].

It examines induction-score trajectories, but does not measure later-token loss relative to earlier tokens, a sharp in-context-learning gain, or a training-loss bump, and therefore does not test whether these occur at the same time as induction-head formation.
The study does not measure how much in-context learning in large transformers is carried by induction heads.
The reported induction-score results concern Pythia-derived models only; other model families, non-transformer architectures, and other modalities are not tested.
The study varies the timing of loss upweighting for induction-pattern tokens, but does not systematically vary training-data properties or compare data setups for persistence of in-context learning.
The study does not compare few-shot task learning with copying or test whether other mechanisms carry most few-shot learning.
The study does not test whether induction-head formation consists of multiple separate or overlapping transitions.

rows.value: figure only; text says the induction score for heads that become induction heads begins to rise right before the BIF increase
rows.note: The authors describe the induction score as a standard metric for how strongly a head implements the induction algorithm. The run used different data ordering and hardware from the original Pythia-14M run.
rows.check: Drop V1. Pythia-14M has MLPs and is not attention-only. The induction score shows attention behaviour, not composition with a previous-token head. For V4, heads with induction behaviour form in this new training run (observed). For V2, abruptness is figure-only: the text says only that the score 'begins to rise right before' the BIF increase. No in-context-learning gain or loss bump is measured, so treat r1's V2 state as cannot_determine.

source_check.correct: V4: observed. V2: cannot_determine for abruptness, a narrow early window, and coincidence with ICL gains or a loss bump. The text reports rising induction scores immediately before the BIF increase, without specifying the score rise's duration or onset.
source_check.problem: The single observed state overstates the evidence for V2; it fits V4.

rows.subject: 3-million parameter transformer
rows.operation_detail: Tracked the maximum induction score across Layer 1 heads without upweighting
rows.measure: Maximum induction score across Layer 1 heads
rows.value: Text says the induction circuit emerges gradually and the induction score peaks at timestep 9k
rows.note: The Figure 17 caption instead describes the baseline as naturally forming induction heads at approximately step 7k. The text and caption differ on the stated timing.
rows.check: Drop V1 (composition not tested) and V5 (control run, nothing varied). For V4 the state is observed: induction heads form in the 3M model. For V2 the state should be partial, not reversed. The text says the circuit 'emerges gradually', peaking late (step 9k of 15k), but the Fig. 17 caption says heads form at about step 7k. Gradual emergence is not the opposite of abrupt formation. It weakens the abrupt, early-window description.

source_check.correct: V2: partial; V4: observed. The control circuit emerges gradually, with the induction score peaking at step 9k. Figure 17 describes head formation around step 7k, a different event.
source_check.problem: Partial fits V2 but not V4; the note also treats formation time and score-peak time as conflicting measurements.
